title: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
summary: Multi-factor authentication request generation describes an adversary who already holds a valid password and then attacks the second factor by making the system send approval prompts to the real user. Push authenticators, one-time codes sent by text message, and automated phone calls can all be triggered simply by attempting a login, so an attacker can repeat the attempt until the user gives in. This pressure is commonly called MFA fatigue. The telemetry is far from subtle: identity providers record bursts of unsuccessful sign-ins for one account, many prompts generated in a short window, and a final success from a new location, device, or address. Pairing that success with the failures immediately before it is what separates an attack from a user who simply mistyped a password. Self-service password reset flows that trigger a push before authentication can be abused in the same way.

beginner.definition: This is an attack where someone already knows your password. They try to log in again and again, so your phone keeps asking you to approve the login. They hope you will finally press yes just to stop the noise.
beginner.whyItMatters: A password alone should not be enough to reach an account, and this attack targets that second step. It does not break the technology; it pressures the person. One tired press of approve can hand over a mailbox or a bank account. Because the login uses stolen but valid credentials, nothing looks broken to the system. Teaching people to question unexpected prompts matters as much as any tool.
howItWorks: The attacker gets a working username and password, often from an earlier breach or a fake login page.
They sign in with those details, and the service then asks for a second proof of identity.
That request reaches the real user as a push notification, a text code, or a phone call.
The attacker repeats the login so the prompts arrive in a constant, confusing stream.
Some attackers also call the user and pretend to be the help desk to ask for the code.
When the user finally approves, the attacker holds a valid session and acts as that person.
beginner.example: Think of a block of flats with a buzzer at the front door. The buzzer rings in your flat, and you press the button to let the visitor in. Now imagine someone who knows your flat number stands outside and presses your buzzer fifty times in one night. At first you ignore it. Eventually, half asleep and annoyed, you press the button just to make it stop. You never checked who was there. MFA fatigue attacks work exactly like that. The password got the attacker to the front door, and your tired press of approve opened it. The answer is a rule that you never open the door without checking. A system that stops the buzzing after a few tries also helps.
takeaways: Many unexpected approval prompts in a row are an attack signal, not a glitch.
Use number matching or phishing-resistant methods so a blind approve cannot work.
Report the prompts, change the password, and end existing sessions straight away.

objectives: Explain how an attacker who holds a valid password abuses push notifications to gain access.
Describe what MFA fatigue looks like in identity provider logs.
List authentication methods that resist an approval prompt attack.
Recognise the signs of a help desk impersonation call that asks for a code.
Outline the response steps after a user reports repeated MFA prompts.
